evidence.claim: Lake Huron’s coastal road links lighthouses, bays and maritime history
evidence.quote: Scenic drives, sandy beaches, charming towns, lighthouses, trails, and unforgettable experiences along US-23, the Sunrise Coast Pure Michigan Byway

evidence.claim: bays and maritime history
evidence.quote: Thunder Bay National Marine Sanctuary and Underwater Preserve is a United States National Marine Sanctuary on Lake Huron's Thunder Bay

evidence.claim: North of Standish, US 23 becomes a two-lane coastal drive, following Saginaw Bay and Lake Huron through woods and shore towns.
evidence.quote: Non-freeway segments of US 23 in the state are two lanes.

evidence.claim: The Sunrise Coast Pure Michigan Byway promotes its sandy beaches, lighthouses and trails along more than 200 miles of Lake Huron shoreline.
evidence.quote: 200+ miles of Lake Huron Shoreline

evidence.claim: The highway north of Standish received its scenic designation in 2004 as the Sunrise Side Coastal Highway.
evidence.quote: In May 2004, the highway north of Standish was named the Sunrise Side Coastal Highway, a scenic highway designation through what is now called the Pure Michigan Byway Program.

evidence.claim: North of Standish, US 23 becomes a two-lane coastal drive, following Saginaw Bay and Lake Huron through woods and shore towns.
evidence.quote: US 23 runs through woods as it follows the Saginaw Bays shoreline northeasterly through Alabaster to Tawas City.

evidence.claim: sandy beaches, lighthouses and trails
evidence.quote: Scenic drives, sandy beaches, charming towns, lighthouses, trails, and unforgettable experiences along US-23

evidence.claim: US 23 began in 1926 with a more inland course between Standish and Mackinaw City.
evidence.quote: From Standish to Mackinaw City, US 23 initially took a more inland route through the northeastern Lower Peninsula.

evidence.claim: Around 1932, the state moved the Omer–Tawas City section onto the Saginaw Bay shore through Au Gres.
evidence.quote: US 23 was moved from its inland routing between Omer and Tawas City via Whittemore to follow a shoreline alignment by way of Au Gres along Saginaw Bay around 1932

evidence.claim: Other relocations followed during the 1930s, and in 1940 the highway took its present lakeshore route between Rogers City and Cheboygan.
evidence.quote: US 23 was moved to its current lakeshore routing between Rogers City and Cheboygan in 1940

evidence.claim: US 23 began in 1926
evidence.quote: US 23 was commissioned on November 11, 1926, with the debut of the United States Numbered Highway System.

evidence.claim: Other relocations followed during the 1930s
evidence.quote: A few years later in 1936, US 23 replaced M-72 between Oscoda and Harrisville and followed a new roadway north to the Spruce area.

evidence.claim: Heading north from Standish, pass through Omer and Au Gres, then follow the bay toward Tawas City and East Tawas.
evidence.quote: Running through Omer, the highway crosses the Rifle River

evidence.claim: The road follows Lake Huron to Oscoda, crosses the Au Sable River, and continues past Harrisville toward Thunder Bay and Alpena.
evidence.quote: The highway intersects the eastern terminus of M-55, runs north and east around Tawas Bay to East Tawas and follows the Lake Huron shoreline to Oscoda.

evidence.claim: Beyond Alpena, it curves past Long Lake and Grand Lake before returning to Lake Huron near Thompson’s Harbor State Park.
evidence.quote: The highway leaves town and runs through rural woodlands to the south shore of Long Lake, curving around the eastern side of the lake. Near the northern end of the lake, US 23 crosses into Presque Isle County and runs along the west shore of Grand Lake. At the north end of that lake, the highway turns west along the Lake Huron shoreline near Thompson's Harbor State Park.

evidence.claim: US 23 bypasses downtown Rogers City, then follows the coast through Cheboygan to Mackinaw City.
evidence.quote: The trunkline continues to Rogers City where it bypasses town to the south and west

evidence.quote: the highway crosses the Au Sable River near its mouth

evidence.claim: continues past Harrisville toward Thunder Bay and Alpena.
evidence.quote: The highway shifts a bit further inland north of Harrisville, continuing to parallel the railroad through the Mackinaw State Forest. Near Ossineke, the trunkline turns back toward the lake, running along the shoreline of Thunder Bay.

evidence.claim: The first Tawas Point lighthouse lost its useful position because the land kept growing.
evidence.quote: The lighthouse was so far inland that mariners were unable to see the lighthouse's light.

evidence.claim: Commissioned in 1853, it stood on a point that shifting sand extended by nearly a mile.
evidence.quote: the lighthouse was commissioned in 1853. After the lighthouse was built, many problems were encountered. Shifting sands caused the point to be extended by nearly a mile.

evidence.claim: Congress approved funding for a replacement in 1875, and the new lighthouse was completed in 1877.
evidence.quote: In 1875 Congress approved a $30,000 amount for a brand new lighthouse. They finished building the lighthouse sometime in 1877.

evidence.claim: The second tower rises 70 feet including its base, with inner and outer brick walls separated by an air space.
evidence.quote: The tower is 70 feet (21 m) tall including the base

evidence.claim: A Fourth Order Fresnel lens remains in place.
evidence.quote: In October 2015, the Coast Guard announced that it would remove the Fresnel lens and replace it with a modern optic beacon. But after public comments, the lens remains in place.

evidence.claim: inner and outer brick walls separated by an air space.
evidence.quote: It is constructed of a brick outer wall, and an inner wall: 24 inches/8 inches thick, respectively. There is an air space between walls of 24 inches (610 mm).

evidence.claim: A Fourth Order Fresnel lens
evidence.quote: The tower has in place a Fourth Order Fresnel lens

evidence.claim: Off Alpena, Thunder Bay’s protected shipwrecks range from nineteenth-century wooden paddle steamers to twentieth-century steel-hulled steamers.
evidence.quote: historically significant shipwrecks ranging from nineteenth-century wooden side-wheeler paddle steamers to twentieth-century steel-hulled steamers.

evidence.claim: The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration established the sanctuary in June 2000, making it the first national marine sanctuary on the Great Lakes.
evidence.quote: The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration established Thunder Bay National Marine Sanctuary and Underwater Preserve on June 22, 2000. It became the thirteenth national marine sanctuary overall and first on the Great Lakes.

evidence.claim: In 2014, its protected area expanded from 448 to 4,300 square miles.
evidence.quote: Original boundaries followed that of Alpena County to 83 degrees west longitude totaling 448 square miles (338 sq nmi; 1,160 km2). In 2014 it was expanded to 4,300 square miles (11,137 km2).

evidence.claim: On the Thunder Bay River in Alpena, the Great Lakes Maritime Heritage Center presents exhibits on local wrecks and the lakes, alongside an archaeological conservation laboratory and education spaces.
evidence.quote: The museum, located in Alpena on the Thunder Bay River, features exhibits about local shipwrecks and the Great Lakes, an auditorium, an archaeological conservation laboratory, and education areas.

evidence.claim: Off Alpena
evidence.quote: Offshore of Alpena is the Thunder Bay National Marine Sanctuary

evidence.claim: Old Presque Isle Light combines two-thirds stone with one-third brick.
evidence.quote: supported physically by two-thirds stone and one-third brick

evidence.claim: Built in 1840, its tower and dwelling deteriorated in harsh weather until Congress found a new station necessary in 1867.
evidence.quote: built in 1840, supported physically by two-thirds stone and one-third brick, and supported financially by funds appropriated by Congress two years earlier of $5,000. The tower and dwelling did not last long in the harsh weather, however, and by 1867 they were deteriorated enough for Congress to find need for a newer station.

evidence.claim: The Lighthouse Board chose a location about two miles north so vessels farther offshore could see the light.
evidence.quote: decided to move the lighthouse location about 2 miles (3.2 km) north, where vessels which were farther from shore could still easily see the light.

evidence.claim: The new tower was designed to stand 113 feet tall, more than 80 feet above the old tower’s height.
evidence.quote: The tower was also designed to be 113 feet (34 m) in height, more than 80 feet (24 m) taller than the older one.

evidence.claim: The old light is no longer operational and serves as a museum; both lighthouses stand on the peninsula east of Grand Lake.
evidence.quote: It presently is not operational and is a museum.

evidence.claim: both lighthouses stand on the peninsula east of Grand Lake.
evidence.quote: This lighthouse and its sister, the New Presque Isle Light, are east of Grand Lake (Presque Ile, Michigan), and sit on the peninsula.

evidence.claim: The last gravel section, near Hammond Bay, was paved in late 1947 or early 1948, completing another stage of the road’s transformation.
evidence.quote: in late 1947 or early 1948; at the same time, the last gravel section of the highway was paved near Hammond Bay in northwestern Presque Isle County.

evidence.claim: The point was originally called Ottawa Point; its name changed officially in 1902.
evidence.quote: It was originally known as Ottawa Point. The name was officially changed to Tawas Point in 1902.

evidence.claim: The sanctuary stretches east from the lakeshore to the international border.
evidence.quote: The sanctuary extends east from the lakeshore to the international border.

evidence.claim: Congress had appropriated $5,000 for the original light two years before it was built.
evidence.quote: built in 1840, supported physically by two-thirds stone and one-third brick, and supported financially by funds appropriated by Congress two years earlier of $5,000.

evidence.claim: Tawas Bay, behind the point, offers shelter from storms, wind and waves coming from the north and northeast.
evidence.quote: Additionally, because it is tucked behind the point, Tawas Bay is an ideal shelter from storms, wind and waves out of the north and northeast.
